The retail decision · Data to decisions

Meet the decision before the methods.

You are advising a retail operations director on whether, where, and how to expand replenishment alerts.

The action the company is considering

Each week, an alert identifies low-stock products for a store team to review before replenishment. The team can bring forward orders where appropriate. Management wants a reliable service improvement that covers the extra service and inventory cost.

Your role is to keep that decision visible as the evidence changes. At first, the data establish the scale of the problem. Later, they support forecasts and evaluate the policy through different study designs.

One outcome and one accounting rule

Each store monitors 20 products for seven days: 140 scheduled product-days per store-week. A stockout product-day records one monitored product unavailable on one day. The primary outcome is the count divided by 140, expressed as a percentage. The service target is 10%.

Stockout rate (%) = stockout product-days ÷ 140 × 100

The accounting scenario charges 6 CU per stockout product-day. Alerts cost 12 CU in service fees and 8 CU in extra holding cost per store-week. These are explicit business assumptions for the spending calculation; they are not a measure of recovered sales.

Weekly accounting cost = 6 × stockout product-days + 20 when alerts are offered

Learn from distinct studies inside one business

The business history behind the lessons
ReleaseWhenWho and why
Operating baselineWeeks 1–16All 150 stores; repaired weeks 1–8 form store profiles
Independent shelf auditWeek 1630 randomly sampled stores; a new measurement of current availability
Forecast exerciseTarget weeks 3–16Train 3–7 / 3–9 / 3–11; validate 8–9 / 10–11 / 12–13; refit 3–13; evaluate 14–16
Randomized pilotWeeks 17–24S001–S050; 25 random offers, 25 usual-operation stores
Voluntary adoptionStarts week 17; assess 17–24S051–S100; adoption follows starting conditions
Later rolloutStarts week 25; assess 25–32S101–S150; 25 selected adopters and 25 comparisons

Every store has the same ID throughout the course. The three intervention cohorts are disjoint; a random offer in the pilot is never treated as voluntary adoption or as the selected later rollout. The forecast uses only the pre-policy period.

Use one set of teaching materials

Start with the motivating business question, then study the general theory before opening the worked application. Each lecture teaches definitions, notation, method, and interpretation in a continuous conceptual sequence. The retail case then supplies the data and calculations. A final synthesis identifies the general lesson and updates the management recommendation.

Choose Present lesson to teach directly from the page. Arrow keys move through the material; Notes displays the fuller explanation in paragraphs; Read this section returns to that exact place in the reading view. The same button is available in the technical continuations.

When you want to inspect a specification or reproduce a calculation, follow the technical link beside that calculation. The continuation shows the same analysis with executable code and a topic map to the supplied original slides. Existing guided-page bookmarks lead to the same complete lesson.

Your final deliverable

Prepare a recommendation that identifies the stores covered, the expected service improvement, its uncertainty, the cost rule, and the next operating action. Use the three intervention studies as evidence about their own populations. Explain how you would learn during the next phase of expansion.

Three checkpoints build an independent recommendation

Each lesson follows explain → reconstruct → diagnose → transfer. Begin with the student notebook, then consult its separate solution. The completed reference lab remains an auditable worked example. Record revisions to your reasoning rather than replacing your first answer silently.

After Lesson 3: measurement and audit memo

Submit a one-page memo with the observation key, denominator, reporting coverage, a repair log and a descriptive plot. Use the unresolved-data exercise to distinguish a sensitivity range from a sampling interval. State the audit target, independent unit, planned precision and budget. A sound answer can conclude that the measurement is not yet adequate for a spending decision.

After Lesson 6: forecast and operating protocol

Submit a dated prediction contract, a training/validation diagram, a benchmark comparison and a five-review workload calculation. Explain which data are available before each forecast. Report the final holdout once, label the added queue check exploratory, and propose a future evaluation period. Specify the action and the experiment needed to learn whether the action helps.

After Lesson 10: expansion and evaluation plan

Submit a two-page decision memo and a reproducible analysis appendix. Compare the populations and assumptions of the pilot, adjusted adoption study and rollout. Name the eligible next-phase stores, capacity, intervention cost, uncertainty and evidence that could reverse the decision. Use the capstone brief and rubric; a defended delay or narrower expansion is acceptable.

Core probability route: Lesson 2 teaches a count table, proportions, conditioning and weighted expectations. Lesson 3 extends this to repeated samples and distributions of estimates. Detailed probability families and Bayes calculations remain optional appendix material.
